land.text: the former Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata as far as the Junta of 25 May 1810 held it: Buenos Aires and the Argentine provinces, with the Banda Oriental in revolt against Montevideo

predecessors.note: The page: after the May Revolution 'the intendancies of La Paz, Chuquisaca...' were 'annexed by the Viceroyalty of Peru'; Paraguay was lost in 1811.

land.text: the Argentine provinces under the Federal Pact of 4 January 1831; the page: 'It was the name of the country from 1831 to 1852'

successors.note: The Argentine Confederation page dates the Federal Pact to 4 January 1831 and the infobox of this page gives 1810-1831; Cliopatria carries this row to 1833 and starts its Argentine Confederation row in 1834.

land.text: Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Misiones, Santa Fe, Córdoba and the Eastern Province, 1815-1820

successors.note: A partial secession (1815), absorbed again in 1820 (infobox 'Succeeded by: 1815 Federal League').

land.text: Paraguay, whose independence the treaty of 12 October 1811 acknowledged
the Eastern Bank, 'an independent state' in 1828 after British intervention (Montevideo Treaty of 28 August 1828)
Upper Peru, which 'was never retaken, and became Bolivia years later'; infobox 'Succeeded by: 1825 Upper Peru'

capitals.name: Buenos Aires
capitals.note: Infobox capital Buenos Aires; the page also mentions Montevideo as declared capital of the Viceroyalty without a date. The Directory (31 January 1814) and the 1816 Congress of Tucumán sat at other towns for periods the page does not give.

correction.text: Buenos Aires and the provinces that recognised the Primera Junta of 25 May 1810, without the Banda Oriental, whose Montevideo government 'did not acknowledge Buenos Aires' government either'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's row begins in 1811 but the page dates the Primera Junta to 25 May 1810 ('The Primera Junta, founded on 25 May 1810') in Buenos Aires. The Banda Oriental is left out for 1810 because Montevideo 'did not acknowledge Buenos Aires' government either'; its war begins with the Cry of Asencio on 28 February 1811. The page gives no area.

correction.text: without western Rio Grande do Sul: the Misiones Orientales were Portuguese under the Treaty of Badajoz (1801) and no page opened shows United Provinces control east of the Uruguay River

keyframe_review.note: 1.68 M km2 (infobox: no area, only population 507,951 in 1816). The shape reaches 131,761 km2 into western Rio Grande do Sul (521 cells, lon -57.5 to -53.3, lat -32.5 to -27.4); the Misiones Orientales page says the Missions were 'definitively ceded to Portugal in the Treaty of Badajoz (1801)' and no page opened shows United Provinces control east of the Uruguay River, so the slice is removed (confidence 2: the page covers the Missions, not the whole slice). The Banda Oriental (Uruguay, 99 percent of the country) stays in the shape but is contested ground from 28 February 1811 (ledger contest events); Paraguay (independent by treaty 12 October 1811) and Upper Peru are already outside it.

correction.text: without western Rio Grande do Sul (the Missions Portuguese since 1801)

keyframe_review.note: Same outline as 1811 (1.68 M km2), so the same Rio Grande do Sul slice is removed; the Second Triumvirate (8 October 1812) and the Second Siege of Montevideo (September 1812) of the UP page leave the Banda Oriental a contested zone.

1.22 M km2: the Banda Oriental is gone from the shape (Uruguay 5 percent) and the Chaco with it. The page has Alvear occupy Montevideo on 23 June 1814 after the Spanish surrender of 20 June, so the United Provinces held the city from 23 June 1814 (ledger); Artigas's countryside is the Federal League's 1814 shape. Entre Ríos, Corrientes and Misiones are still inside; the page does not date when they passed to Artigas ('Misiones embraced federalism ... near February 1814'). Unverified beyond that: page budget.

0.91 M km2 for 1815-1819: Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Misiones, most of Santa Fe and the Eastern Province are the Federal League's (members: Córdoba with La Rioja, Corrientes, Entre Ríos, Misiones, the Eastern Province and Santa Fe; 'in 1815 declared the Liga Federal'). Cliopatria splits Córdoba 70/24 between the two states and leaves La Rioja with the United Provinces; the page gives no join dates, so the split stands as drawn.

1.39 M km2: after Cepeda (1 February 1820) the Federal League land is back inside the outline although the page calls the result the fall of the Supreme Directorship and the start of the 'caudillo era'; the provinces governed themselves ('each province began to govern itself', Argentine Confederation page). Entre Ríos and Corrientes were the Republic of Entre Ríos from 29 September 1820 to September-October 1821 (ledger; Republic of Entre Ríos page). The outline is the loose alliance of provinces, drawn soft.

1.41 M km2 for 1822-1827, the same provinces; the page: 'Between 1820 and 1826, the United Provinces functioned as a loose alliance of autonomous provinces'. The Banda Oriental (Cisplatina, Empire of Brazil's shape) is outside; it is contested 1825-1828 (ledger). The growth of 19,000 km2 over 1820 is not explained by any page opened.

1.41 M km2 for 1828-1829. The shape's southern bbox edge drops from 37.1 to 41.1 degrees S; no page opened mentions the land there, so the change is unexplained and the shape stands. 1827: 'the constitution stopped being applied'; the infobox lists 1827-1831 as a de facto confederation.

Identical to 1828-1829 (1.41 M km2) for 1830-1833. The Federal Pact is dated 4 January 1831 and the Argentine Confederation 'was the name of the country from 1831 to 1852'; Cliopatria keeps this row to 1833 and begins its Argentine Confederation row in 1834, so no land changes at the rename.

region.text: Buenos Aires and the provinces that recognised the Primera Junta of 25 May 1810, without the Banda Oriental, whose Montevideo government 'did not acknowledge Buenos Aires' government either'

ledger.note: 25 May 1810: the Primera Junta takes power at Buenos Aires. 'The Primera Junta, founded on 25 May 1810, was a government junta similar to the ones from the Iberian Peninsula.' The page names Buenos Aires, not a boundary; the core is read as the provinces without the Banda Oriental.

region.text: Upper Peru: the intendancies of La Paz, Chuquisaca ... (today Bolivia)

ledger.note: 1811: the first campaign into Upper Peru. The page dates only its end ('on 20 June 1811, the First Upper Peru campaign would be sealed as a failure') and says the intendancies of La Paz and Chuquisaca were 'annexed by the Viceroyalty of Peru after the May Revolution'; the start date is page-silent.

region.text: the Eastern Bank of the Uruguay River

ledger.note: 28 February 1811: the Cry of Asencio begins the Oriental Revolution. 'On 28 February 1811, the Cry of Asencio took place, marking the beginning of the Oriental Revolution'; Montevideo 'did not acknowledge Buenos Aires' government either' and the Junta's squadron was destroyed at San Nicolas. Montevideo's royalists and the revolution share the Banda Oriental.

12 October 1811: the first treaty acknowledges Paraguay's independence. 'The first one acknowledged Paraguay's independence from Buenos Aires' after the Paraguay campaign 'was defeated'. The 1811 Cliopatria shape already excludes Paraguay.

22 November 1811: the First Triumvirate adopts 'United Provinces of the Río de la Plata'. 'This name was officially adopted by the First Triumvirate on 22 November 1811.' The Triumvirate had been established on 23 September 1811.

region.text: the Eastern Bank, after the fall of Montevideo

ledger.note: 20-23 June 1814: Montevideo falls to Buenos Aires. 'after almost four years of conflict, Captain General of Montevideo Gaspar de Vigodet negotiated the surrender'; 'On 23 June 1814, Alvear ... occupied the city.'

region.text: Montevideo, the last Spanish stronghold on the Eastern Bank

ledger.note: 23 June 1814: Alvear occupies Montevideo. 'On 23 June 1814, Alvear ... occupied the city.' Only the city and its surroundings; Cliopatria's Federal League 1814 shape covers the rest of the Eastern Bank.

region.text: Córdoba (with La Rioja), Corrientes, Entre Ríos, Misiones and Santa Fe, the Federal League's provinces west of the Uruguay

ledger.note: 1815: the provinces of the Federal League leave Buenos Aires. 'in 1815 declared the Liga Federal'; the members are Córdoba (with La Rioja), Corrientes, Entre Ríos, Misiones, the Eastern Province and Santa Fe. The page gives no join dates.

10 January 1815: Guayabos brings the Eastern Bank into the Federal League. 'The federal victory at Guayabos on 10 January 1815 brought the Eastern Bank into the Federal League.' Montevideo, which Alvear had occupied in June 1814, lies on the Eastern Bank.

29 November 1815: Viluma ends the Upper Peru campaigns. 'Rondeau was defeated and the campaign was sealed as a failure' at Viluma; the page: Upper Peru was 'never retaken, and became Bolivia years later'.

9 July 1816: the Congress of Tucumán declares independence. 'On 9 July 1816, after long arguments, the deputies finally declared independence' from Ferdinand VII; the state styles itself the United Provinces in South America. Delegates of the Federal League provinces were turned away.

region.text: the Federal League provinces west of the Uruguay

ledger.note: 1 February 1820: Cepeda ends the Federal League's separate existence. The League 'effectively came to an end as a separate political entity'; the Directorship fell and the Treaty of Pilar was signed on 23 February. Cliopatria puts the League's provinces back inside the 1820 outline, though the page calls the result the start of the 'caudillo era' with autonomous provinces.

region.text: the Republic of Entre Ríos: Entre Ríos and Corrientes

ledger.note: 29 September 1820: Ramírez founds the Republic of Entre Ríos. Infobox: 'Established: September 29 1820'; the Cepeda page: Ramírez 'declared the Republic of Entre Ríos on September 29, 1820.' The republic covered land in the modern provinces of Entre Ríos and Corrientes (Ramírez occupied Corrientes on 19 September 1820). Cliopatria draws both inside the Río de la Plata outline throughout.

28 September 1821: Entre Ríos returns to the provincial alliance. Colonel Lucio Norberto Mansilla rebelled in Paraná on 23 September 1821 with the backing of Santa Fe and a Buenos Aires squadron and had himself elected governor on 28 September, the infobox date of the republic's end; the page has Mansilla allied with Buenos Aires after taking power. The Cepeda page dates Ramírez's death to 10 July 1821.

12 October 1821: Corrientes declares itself an autonomous federated province. Its civic leaders deposed Carriego and named Atienza provisional governor, who announced its autonomy the same day; Ferré's troops reached the city on 18 October. Cliopatria keeps Corrientes inside the outline, so the gain is nominal: the provinces governed themselves after 1820 ('each province began to govern itself', Argentine Confederation page).

25 October 1825: the Argentine Congress takes in the Banda Oriental. The Congress 'proclaimed the Cisplatina province reintegrated into the United Provinces on 25 October 1825', after the Thirty-Three Orientals landed on 19 April 1825 and the Florida assembly declared union on 25 August 1825. Brazil declared war on 10 December 1825; the Cisplatina is the Empire of Brazil's land in Cliopatria.

region.text: Cisplatina, independent as the Eastern Republic of Uruguay

ledger.note: 27 August 1828: the Preliminary Peace Convention makes Uruguay independent. 'The conflict continued until 27 August 1828'; the treaty 'acknowledged the independence of Cisplatina under the name Eastern Republic of Uruguay'.

4 January 1831: the Federal Pact. The infobox gives 'Federal Pact: 4 January 1831' and the page says Argentine Confederation 'was the name of the country from 1831 to 1852'. The United Provinces of this row become the Argentine Confederation by usage.

region.text: the provinces of the Argentine Confederation

ledger.note: 1833: Cliopatria's United Provinces row ends. The pages date the end of the United Provinces to the Federal Pact of 1831 and start the Argentine Confederation then; Cliopatria starts its Argentine Confederation row in 1834, so the dossier keeps the shape to 1833 and hands it on. No border changes.

wars.name: Paraguay campaign
wars.outcome: Buenos Aires' expedition 'was defeated'; the treaty of 12 October 1811 acknowledged Paraguay's independence.
wars.note: The page gives no campaign dates; the treaty date is the one it gives.

wars.name: Upper Peru campaigns
wars.outcome: The first campaign failed after Huaqui (20 June 1811) and Rondeau was defeated at Viluma on 29 November 1815; Upper Peru stayed royalist and became Bolivia.
wars.note: The second campaign (1813) is not on the page.

wars.name: Oriental Revolution and the sieges of Montevideo
wars.outcome: Cry of Asencio 28 February 1811; the October 1811 treaty acknowledged the viceroy's authority over the Eastern Bank; the Second Siege began in September 1812; Vigodet surrendered on 20 June 1814 and Alvear occupied Montevideo on 23 June.

wars.name: Battle of Cepeda (1820)
wars.outcome: The Federals (Santa Fe, Entre Ríos) defeated the national government under Supreme Director Rondeau on 1 February 1820; the Treaty of Pilar followed on 23 February; the League ended and the caudillo era began.

wars.name: Cisplatine War
wars.outcome: Brazil declared war on 10 December 1825; there was fighting at Sarandí (12 October 1825) and Ituzaingó/Passo do Rosário (20 February 1827), the Argentines defeated the Brazilian flotilla at Juncal and the Brazilian blockade of Buenos Aires caused 'severe economic consequences'; the Preliminary Peace Convention of 27 August 1828 made Cisplatina independent as Uruguay.

certainty.note: No survey or treaty line fixes any frontier of the United Provinces on land: the Andean, Chaco, Patagonian and Banda Oriental limits are approximate, and from 1820 to 1826 the page calls the state 'a loose alliance of autonomous provinces'. The 1828 Preliminary Peace Convention fixes the Uruguay line but is not this state's border.

notes: Cliopatria's row 'Río de la Plata' (1811-1833) is the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, i.e. the Buenos Aires-led state of the May Revolution; its Wikipedia field 'Río de la Plata' and Wikidata Q35827 point at the estuary, not the state, so identity.wikipedia is the state's own article and wikidata keeps Cliopatria's id. The Argentine Confederation row starts in 1834 and the pages date the Confederation to the Federal Pact of 4 January 1831; the dossier keeps the Cliopatria years (dissolve at 1833, confidence 1) and the rendering agent may prefer to hand the land over in 1831. Cliopatria's 1811-1813 shapes include 131,761 km2 of western Rio Grande do Sul; the Misiones Orientales page has the Missions Portuguese since 1801 and no page opened shows United Provinces control east of the Uruguay River, so both verdicts remove the slice (confidence 2). The infobox gives no area, only population (507,951 in 1816). Not settled: when Entre Ríos, Corrientes and Misiones passed to Artigas (page: 'near February 1814'); the Army of the Andes and the Chile campaign (the page gives no date); the cause of the 1828 southward growth. The Republic of Entre Ríos (29 September 1820 - September/October 1821, Entre Ríos and Corrientes, Ramírez) is written as republic-of-entre-rios; Cliopatria lacks it and keeps both provinces inside the outline. The Falkland Islands (invaded by the United Kingdom at the end of 1832 per the Argentine Confederation page) are outside every shape.
